title: How Source Code Becomes Machine Code
summary: The CPU only understands numbers, so C++ has to be translated before it can run. Four tools do it in turn: the **preprocessor**, the **compiler**, the **assembler** and the **linker**. Knowing what each one does explains most build errors and almost everything you will see in a debugger.
markdown:
## From text to numbers In lesson 1.01 the tiny computer ran a program that was nothing but numbers in memory. A real CPU is the same. It has never heard of C++. A `.cpp` file is text for people, and something has to turn it into the numbers the processor executes. That job is split into stages. Each stage takes one kind of file and produces another. ```mermaid flowchart LR SRC["main.cpp
your source"] --> PRE["Preprocessor
pastes in headers,
expands macros"] PRE --> COMP["Compiler
C++ to
assembly"] COMP --> ASM["Assembler
assembly to
machine code"] ASM --> OBJ["main.obj
object file"] OBJ --> LINK["Linker
joins object files
and libraries"] LIB["Libraries
(.lib)"] --> LINK LINK --> EXE["game.exe"] ``` When you press Build in Visual Studio, all of these run one after another, so it feels like one step. It is worth knowing the stages apart, because each has its own kind of error. ## Stage 1: the preprocessor Every line that starts with `#` is an instruction to the **preprocessor**, which works on plain text before any C++ is understood. | Directive | What the preprocessor does | |---|---| | `#include ` | Pastes the whole of that file in place of the line | | `#define MAX_PLAYERS 4` | From here on, replaces the word `MAX_PLAYERS` with `4` | | `#ifdef _DEBUG` ... `#endif` | Keeps or drops the lines in between, depending on whether `_DEBUG` is defined | The result is one long file called a **translation unit**. Including `` alone adds tens of thousands of lines. You never see this file, but the compiler does. ```cpp #include #define GREETING "Hello from the preprocessor" #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)) int main() { std::cout << GREETING << '\n'; std::cout << SQUARE(7) << '\n'; #ifdef _DEBUG std::cout << "This is a debug build\n"; #endif return 0; } ``` ``` Hello from the preprocessor 49 This is a debug build ``` The examples on this site are built as Debug builds, where `_DEBUG` is defined, so the last line appears. In a Release build the preprocessor removes that line before the compiler ever sees it. By the time the compiler sees `main`, the second line reads `std::cout << ((7) * (7)) << '\n';`. The word `SQUARE` is gone. Macros are text substitution and nothing more, which is why modern C++ prefers `constexpr` variables and ordinary functions: those obey the language's rules for types and scope. > [!tip] See the preprocessed file yourself > In Visual Studio, open the project's properties, go to **C/C++ → Preprocessor** and set **Preprocess to a File** to Yes. Building then writes `main.i`, the text the compiler actually reads. Turn the option off again afterwards, because it stops the build from producing an executable. ## Stage 2: the compiler The **compiler** reads the translation unit, checks that it is valid C++, and translates every function into **assembly language**: a text form of machine instructions, one per line. This is the stage that reports most of the errors you meet, such as a missing semicolon, a type that does not match, or a name that does not exist. Here is a small function and what Microsoft's compiler turns it into, with optimisation switched on: ```cpp int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } ``` ```asm addBonus PROC lea eax, DWORD PTR [rcx+50] ret 0 addBonus ENDP ``` Two instructions. The argument `score` arrived in a register called `rcx`, the result is left in a register called `eax`, and `ret` returns to whoever called the function. You do not need to read assembly yet: chapter 7 teaches it properly. For now, notice that each line is one small action, just like the tiny computer's instructions. ## Stage 3: the assembler The **assembler** turns each assembly line into its numeric encoding. `ret` becomes the single byte `C3`. The `lea` line becomes three bytes, `8D 41 32`, and the `32` at the end is 50 in hexadecimal: the bonus itself, stored inside the instruction. ``` addBonus: 8D 41 32 lea eax, [rcx+32h] C3 ret ``` This is exactly what lesson 1.01 described: a program is numbers in memory. These four bytes *are* the function `addBonus`. When the game runs, they sit somewhere in memory, and calling `addBonus` means telling the CPU to fetch its next instruction from there. The assembler's output is an **object file** (`.obj` on Windows). It holds the machine code for one `.cpp` file, plus a list of names it defines and names it uses but does not define. ## Stage 4: the linker A real program is many `.cpp` files, and each one is compiled on its own. If `main.cpp` calls `addBonus` but `addBonus` lives in `score.cpp`, then `main.obj` contains a call to a function whose address it does not know. It leaves a note: "fill in the address of `addBonus` here". The **linker** reads every object file and every library, matches each "I need" note with the "I define" entry that answers it, fills in the real addresses, and writes the final `.exe`. ```mermaid flowchart LR M["main.obj
defines: main
needs: addBonus, printf"] --> L["Linker"] S["score.obj
defines: addBonus"] --> L C["C runtime library
defines: printf, ..."] --> L L --> E["game.exe
every call has a real address"] ``` That explains the two classic linker errors: | Error | Meaning | |---|---| | `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol addBonus` | Something needs `addBonus`, and no object file or library defines it. Often a `.cpp` file is missing from the project, or a library was not added. | | `LNK2005: addBonus already defined in main.obj` | Two object files both define it. Often a function body was written in a header that two `.cpp` files include. | Neither is a mistake in the C++ syntax, which is why they only appear after compiling has succeeded. ## Why the stages matter later Everything in the rest of this course rests on this pipeline. - **Debugging.** The debugger shows you the running machine code and maps it back to your source lines using a separate file of **debug symbols** (`.pdb`) that the compiler and linker write alongside the program. - **Assembly.** Chapter 7 reads the compiler's output, the stage 2 text you saw above. - **Libraries and DLLs.** Chapter 4 shows how the linker can leave some addresses to be filled in when the program starts, which is how DLLs work. - **Reverse engineering.** Chapter 9 runs the pipeline backwards: from the numbers in an `.exe` back to something a person can understand. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Thinking `#include` is like `import` in other languages > It is a literal copy and paste of text. Including the same header twice pastes it twice, which is why headers start with `#pragma once`. > [!warning] Putting function bodies in headers without `inline` > Each `.cpp` that includes the header gets its own copy of the function, and the linker reports `already defined`. Put the body in a `.cpp` file, or mark it `inline`. > [!warning] Reading a linker error as a syntax error > If the message starts with `LNK`, your code compiled. Look for a missing file, a missing library, or a declaration that does not match its definition exactly. > [!warning] Macros with missing brackets > `#define SQUARE(x) x * x` turns `SQUARE(2 + 3)` into `2 + 3 * 2 + 3`, which is 11. This is one reason to prefer `constexpr` functions. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Name the four stages of a build, in order. - Compiler, preprocessor, linker, assembler - Preprocessor, compiler, linker, assembler + Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker - Compiler, assembler, preprocessor, linker > The first three run once per `.cpp` file; the linker runs once for the whole program, joining the object files. ? Why is each `.cpp` file compiled separately? + So that changing one file only means recompiling that one file - So that each file can be written in a different language - Because the compiler can only hold one file in memory at a time - So that each file becomes a separate program > The linker then joins the pieces. A consequence is that one file cannot see another's definitions, only the declarations it includes. ? What is the difference between a compiler error and a linker error? + A compiler error means one file is not valid C++; a linker error means the valid pieces do not fit together - A compiler error is a warning; a linker error stops the build - A linker error means a file has a syntax mistake the compiler missed - A compiler error happens at run time; a linker error happens while building > A linker error such as LNK2019 means something declared was never defined, or something was defined twice. Both kinds of error happen while building. ? What does `.pdb` stand for in Visual Studio, and what is it for? - Program debug binary: a debug copy of the `.exe` - Precompiled database: headers compiled ahead of time to speed up builds - Project definition block: the settings of the project + Program database: the debug symbols linking machine code to source lines and variable names > The debugger needs the `.pdb` to show your own code and variable names instead of raw instructions. Precompiled headers are a different file (`.pch`). ? Which stage turns `#include ` into thousands of lines of code? - The compiler + The preprocessor - The linker > The preprocessor handles every `#` line, and `#include` is a straight paste of the file's text. ? What does an object file (`.obj`) contain? - The finished program, ready to run + One file's machine code, plus the names it defines and needs - The assembly language text for the whole program > Each `.cpp` file becomes one object file. The linker later joins them and fills in the addresses that were missing. ? A build fails with `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol`. What is the most likely cause? - A missing semicolon - A spelling mistake inside a comment + A function is declared and called but never defined > Linker errors appear after compiling has succeeded. Something is used but never defined in anything the linker was given. ? In the assembler output above, why does the byte `32` appear in the encoding of `lea eax, [rcx+50]`? - It is the size of the instruction + 50 in decimal is `0x32` in hexadecimal - It is the address of the function > Numbers inside instructions are stored as bytes like everything else. Fifty is three sixteens and two, which is `0x32`. ```
ideas:
- Run the preprocessor example. Then change `SQUARE(7)` to `SQUARE(3 + 4)`. It still prints 49 because of the brackets in the macro. Remove the brackets from the definition and predict the new answer before you run it.
- In Visual Studio, create a second file `score.cpp` holding `addBonus`, and call it from `main.cpp` with a declaration `int addBonus(int score);` at the top. Build it. Then remove `score.cpp` from the project and read the linker error you get.
- Turn on **Preprocess to a File** for one build and open the `.i` file. Search it for `main` to find your own code at the very bottom.

cards.q: Name the four stages of a build, in order.
cards.a:
Preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker

The first three run once per `.cpp` file; the linker runs once for the whole program, joining the object files.

cards.q: Why is each `.cpp` file compiled separately?
cards.a:
So that changing one file only means recompiling that one file

The linker then joins the pieces. A consequence is that one file cannot see another's definitions, only the declarations it includes.

cards.q: What is the difference between a compiler error and a linker error?
cards.a:
A compiler error means one file is not valid C++; a linker error means the valid pieces do not fit together

A linker error such as LNK2019 means something declared was never defined, or something was defined twice. Both kinds of error happen while building.

cards.q: What does `.pdb` stand for in Visual Studio, and what is it for?
cards.a:
Program database: the debug symbols linking machine code to source lines and variable names

The debugger needs the `.pdb` to show your own code and variable names instead of raw instructions. Precompiled headers are a different file (`.pch`).

cards.q: Which stage turns `#include <vector>` into thousands of lines of code?
cards.a:
The preprocessor

The preprocessor handles every `#` line, and `#include` is a straight paste of the file's text.

cards.q: What does an object file (`.obj`) contain?
cards.a:
One file's machine code, plus the names it defines and needs

Each `.cpp` file becomes one object file. The linker later joins them and fills in the addresses that were missing.

cards.q: A build fails with `LNK2019: unresolved external symbol`. What is the most likely cause?
cards.a:
A function is declared and called but never defined

Linker errors appear after compiling has succeeded. Something is used but never defined in anything the linker was given.

cards.q: In the assembler output above, why does the byte `32` appear in the encoding of `lea eax, [rcx+50]`?
cards.a:
50 in decimal is `0x32` in hexadecimal

Numbers inside instructions are stored as bytes like everything else. Fifty is three sixteens and two, which is `0x32`.
